column4: Those who remain patient seeking the face of their Lord also spend from God's provision secretly and openly, an exceptionally close meeting of the motive and act in 92:18-20.
A single inventory of worldly property includes gold and silver, marked horses, livestock, and cultivated fields, placing herd and crop together as the forms of māl that can captivate their owner.
David and Solomon judge a cultivated field damaged when a people's sheep stray into it by night, a literal meeting between the section's two economic images, herd and crop.
God gives Solomon the right understanding of the sheep-and-field case, so the scene's competing property claims remain subject to divine judgment rather than mere ownership.
The command to glorify the name of رَبِّكَ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ gives the exact divine title sought in 92:20 and supplies the giver's Lordward stance.
The Most High is the one who creates and proportions, connecting 87:1's Rabb to the created male and female and to the section's idea of making a thing fit.
The same Lord determines and guides, bringing measure and hidaya together immediately before the pasture image.
God brings out the pasture, directly staging the vegetation that feeds the section's herd under the care of Rabb al-Aʿlā.
A good word is a good tree with firm roots and branches in heaven; with 14:25 it supplies the full image for the giver who grows as a fruit-bearing tree.
Livestock carry heavy loads to distant places people could scarcely reach themselves, extending the concrete value of the desert herd named in 16:5-6.
Immediately after the livestock-hide dwellings of 16:80, God says He thus completes His favor upon people, matching the section's dictionary claim that Rabb completes niʿma.
One sign-complex contains rain from the sky, revived earth, dispersed animals, and governed clouds, bringing cloud, fertile ground, and herd under one divine ordering.
God says He will complete His favor upon the believers so that they may be guided, joining the section's completed niʿma and hidaya in one promise.
God completes His favor upon the Messenger and guides him on a straight path, another explicit convergence of favor brought to completion and guidance.
God promises increase in response to gratitude, making the true enlargement of blessing a relation to its divine giver.
Men and women who give charity are named in parallel among the faithful qualities God rewards, joining the section's male/female pair directly to almsgiving.
Forgoing one's retaliation claim as charity becomes an expiation for the forgiver, a juridical example of voluntary giving that discharges a liability and cleanses.
Whoever fears God has his affair made easy, tightly joining taqwa to divine yusr as 92:5-7 does.
The one who brings truth and confirms it is identified with the God-fearing, joining ṣ-d-q and taqwa as the positive counterpart to denial.
Prayer and sacrifice, together with life and death, are declared wholly for God, Lord of the worlds, stating the exclusive orientation of the animal offering.
The people are told to fear the one who supplied everything they know, introducing a concrete inventory of livestock and gardens as divine provision.
The provision is specified as livestock and sons, explicitly placing the herd among the favors supplied by God.
Gardens and springs follow the livestock, completing the field-and-herd abundance for which the people owe recognition.
The relative, needy person, and traveler must be given their due, another direct formulation of a right contained within one's provision.
Water descends from the sky in due measure and is lodged in the earth, while God can also remove it; the source of continuing yield is both fitted and revocable.
That measured water grows gardens of palms and grapes with abundant fruit, supplying the exact fruiting increase that the section attaches to itāʾ.
The ayah joins giving zakat, lending God a good loan, and finding with God whatever good one advances, gathering charity, divine receipt, and return.
The face of the Lord possessed of majesty and honor remains after all earthly things pass, identifying the enduring object sought by the giver.
Everything perishes except God's face, making explicit why wealth may be released for the one object that remains.
The pasture is made dark stubble after being brought forth, a precise vegetal counterpart to increase that unexpectedly ceases.
Satan threatens poverty to deter spending while God promises forgiveness and bounty, exposing the two rival expectations behind withholding and giving.
Believers are commanded to leave outstanding usury if they are truthful, drawing the ethical boundary around the apparent financial growth rejected in 2:276.
Only the principal may remain after usury is renounced, so neither party wrongs the other; this defines the non-growing amount against charitable multiplication.
The prohibition on consuming usury multiplied many times makes false financial increase visible as the opposite of the charity God multiplies.
Pagans assign what lies in livestock wombs exclusively to males and forbid it to females, a corrupt herd rule that combines the section's animals, sex distinction, and womb.
People criticize the allocation of charities and are content only when they receive a share, revealing a self-interested stance around the same collection system named in 9:60.
On the Day of Judgment neither wealth nor children benefit, directly repeating the boundary in 92:11 on what māl cannot do when its owner falls.
The condemned person says his wealth did not avail him, an almost exact first-person enactment of 92:11.
Abu Lahab's wealth and acquisitions do not avail him, another direct reversal of confidence in accumulated māl.
The liar who rejects truth is set under judgment, supplying the negative k-dh-b side of the truth-confirming, God-fearing figure in 39:33.
The condemned person neither confirms the truth nor prays, restaging the failed ṣ-d-q stance of 92:9 and 92:16.
Instead he denies and turns away, reproducing in one ayah the paired actions كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ of 92:16.
Those who withhold God's bounty wrongly think stinginess is good for them; what they withheld will encircle them, reversing wealth that purifies when released.
The stingy command others to stinginess and conceal what God gave from His bounty, opposing both acknowledgment of niʿma and voluntary giving.
Wealth and children must not distract believers from remembering God; it introduces the command in 63:10 to spend before death closes the opportunity.
Wealth and children are the adornment of nearer life while enduring righteous deeds are better with the Lord, distinguishing held property from the lasting Godward act.
Qarun's immense treasures make wealth the visible basis of arrogance at the opening of a downfall scene.
Qarun attributes his wealth to his own knowledge, the self-sufficient claim opposite to yield recognized as the Lord's nurture.
The earth swallows Qarun and his house, and no group or self-help saves him, graphically enacting wealth's failure when its owner falls.
Observers then acknowledge that God expands and restricts provision, relocating increase and decrease with the true provider.
The affluent claim that greater wealth and children secure them against punishment, another false inference from visible increase.
Wealth and children do not bring anyone near to God; faith and good action do, distinguishing possessed abundance from the quality that reaches Him.
Everything on earth passes away, the necessary first half of the boundary completed by the enduring face of the Lord in 55:27.
A man with ninety-nine ewes demands his brother's sole ewe, a herd scene in which taking one animal is an unjust seizure rather than the rightful charitable due developed in the section.
David identifies the demand for the lone ewe as wrongdoing and warns that partners often transgress, distinguishing compulsory injustice from a sheep voluntarily or lawfully given.
Those who are stingy and command stinginess are warned that God is self-sufficient, the theological inverse of imagining that retained wealth enriches its owner or that God needs the gift.
Wealth and children are a test immediately before the command to spend, framing property as the arena in which generosity or withholding is disclosed.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are provided for riding and adornment, extending 16:6's beauty-at-the-herd scene to the other animals of desert property.
Date and grape fruits yield both intoxicant and good provision immediately after the livestock-milk ayah, placing animal drink beside the productive fruit tree.
Those involved in charity distribution are told to be content with what God and His Messenger give and to desire God, the receptive counterpart to giving without bargaining.
Those unable to find means for an expedition leave in tears because they have nothing to spend, a specific picture of voluntary expenditure constrained by lack of property.
During famine, Joseph's brothers bring scant merchandise, ask for full measure, and request charity; agricultural scarcity, measured provision, and the giving sense of ṣ-d-q meet.
Within the pilgrimage-sacrifice passage, livestock are declared lawful and false speech forbidden, placing the offered herd beside the truth/denial boundary.
Abraham's son is ransomed with a great sacrifice, a distinct sacrificial-animal scene in which an offering discharges what was otherwise due.
God declares His favor completed upon the community, a direct Quranic formulation of the dictionary sense cited for completing niʿma.
The earth is laid out for living creatures, opening a provision scene of fruit, palms, and grain.
Fruit and date palms with sheathed clusters name the yielding tree behind the source section's itāʾ imagery.
Husked grain and fragrant plants complete the earth's crop provision.
The refrain asks which favors of the Lord can be denied immediately after the crop inventory, joining niʿma, Rabb, and kadhaba around agricultural provision.
Fertilizing winds are sent and water descends for people to drink, offering a natural counterpart to the section's gendered fertility and cloud-grown field.
Moses uses his staff to beat down leaves for his sheep, a remembered Quranic detail of the daily care by which the herd is sustained.
God creates the pair, male and female, repeating the created polarity from which the section extends its agricultural senses.
That pair comes from an emitted drop, adding the reproductive origin behind the male/female formulation.
The human begins as an emitted drop, opening another staged account of sexed creation.
The drop becomes a clot and is created and proportioned, contributing the gradual formation associated with the section's nurture language.
God makes from it the two sexes, male and female, explicitly repeating 92:3.
Human creation begins from an extract of clay, opening a stepwise formation that links earth and embodied growth.
The human is then placed as a drop in a secure resting place, supplying the womb setting recalled in the section.
Successive transformations carry the embryo toward another creation, a Quranic enactment of nurture from state to state toward completion.
God has created human beings in stages, a concise parallel to the section's definition of tarbiya as bringing something through successive states.
Dust, drop, clot, childhood, maturity, and old age form an extended sequence of divinely governed development toward completion.
No soul can discharge anything for another on Judgment Day, a boundary on the source dictionary sense of a sheep or charity sufficing on someone's behalf.
The repeated warning again denies that one soul can suffice for another or that compensation can be accepted, reinforcing the eschatological limit on transferable discharge.
Neither parent nor child can avail the other before the Lord, making family relation itself unable to settle the final liability.
No soul possesses anything for another on that day and command belongs to God, the ultimate boundary around human repayment and substitution.
The Messenger recites, teaches, and purifies the community, supplying a non-financial use in which purification is mediated rather than self-claimed.
The Messenger's recitation and instruction purify believers, clarifying another agent and means of the z-k-w process beside charitable purification.
A messenger among the unlettered recites, purifies, and teaches them, repeating communal purification through revelation rather than wealth.
John receives tenderness and purity from God and is God-fearing, a compact meeting of z-k-w and taqwa as divine gift and human quality.
Whatever believers spend in preparation is fully repaid without injustice, a specific promise of return that contrasts with giving in order to collect a human favor.
What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, supporting the section's transfer of wealth toward the enduring divine face.
